# Get started on PX4 SITL

<!-- type: how-to · level: 1 -->

**Needs first:** [Install](../start/install.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: starter status -->
<!-- END GENERATED starter status -->

This starter puts a nano-ros module into PX4 Autopilot and starts it in
PX4's software-in-the-loop simulator (SITL), which runs the autopilot as an
ordinary program on your Linux machine. There is no flight controller, no
simulator window and no cable. The module joins PX4 the way any downstream
firmware does, as an external module, so you do not fork PX4.

A PX4 module is C++: PX4's module and uORB interfaces are C++ only, so this
starter has no Rust or C tab.

## What you need

- A Linux host with the [install](../start/install.md) done, so `nros` is on
  your `PATH`.
- About 10 GB of disk for the PX4 checkout and its build, and git.
- Ubuntu, for PX4's setup script. On another host, follow PX4's own
  development-environment guide instead of the setup step below.

## Get PX4

PX4 is your own checkout: the firmware tree you would build anyway. nano-ros
is tested against PX4 v1.17.0:

```bash probe=30
git clone --branch v1.17.0 https://github.com/PX4/PX4-Autopilot.git
git -C PX4-Autopilot submodule update --init \
    --depth 1 --recommend-shallow --recursive
```

PX4's own setup script installs its build tools and Python dependencies,
once per host. SITL needs neither the NuttX toolchain nor the simulators, so
leave them out:

```bash probe=32
bash PX4-Autopilot/Tools/setup/ubuntu.sh --no-nuttx --no-sim-tools
```

## Add the nano-ros module

The nano-ros SDK ships a PX4 module template. Copy it out beside the PX4
checkout; PX4 is pointed at the copy when it builds:

```bash probe=40
mkdir -p px4-modules
sdk="$(nros locate nano-ros)"
cp -r "$sdk/integrations/px4/module-template" px4-modules/nano-ros
```

That wrote the layout PX4 requires of an external module:

```text
px4-modules/nano-ros/
└── src/
    ├── CMakeLists.txt              # the external module list
    └── modules/
        └── nano_ros_app/
            ├── CMakeLists.txt      # nros_px4_add_module(... MAIN nano_ros_app)
            └── nano_ros_app.cpp    # the module: edit this one
```

## Build

PX4's own `make` builds one tree, with the module joined in through
`EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION`:

```bash probe=50
make -C PX4-Autopilot px4_sitl_default \
    EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION="$PWD/px4-modules/nano-ros"
```

The module links nano-ros archives the SDK ships prebuilt, so there is no
Rust build step. The first build compiles PX4 itself and takes several
minutes; later ones take seconds.

## Run it in SITL

Start the PX4 daemon from the SITL build directory. With no simulator
attached it boots headless, which is enough to start the module:

```bash probe=60 probe-run=120 probe-keep
cd PX4-Autopilot/build/px4_sitl_default
bin/px4 -d etc/init.d-posix/rcS
```

It is up once its startup script reports:

```text probe-expect=60
Startup script returned successfully
```

In a second terminal, in the same directory, start the module through the
daemon's client command:

```bash probe=70 probe-run=60
cd PX4-Autopilot/build/px4_sitl_default
bin/px4-nano_ros_app start
```

```text probe-expect=70
nano-ros uORB backend registered
```

The module has registered nano-ros's uORB backend with PX4 and returned. The
template forwards nothing on its own: you add the topics it carries in
`nano_ros_app.cpp`. Press Ctrl-C in the first terminal to stop PX4.

## If it doesn't work

- **`make` stops in the module's configure and names a missing archive:**
  the `nros` on your `PATH` belongs to an SDK without the PX4 archives.
  Check `nros locate nano-ros` names the SDK you installed.
- **`bin/px4-nano_ros_app start` says the daemon is not running:** start
  `bin/px4 -d` first, from the same build directory, and wait for its
  startup line.
- **The module logs `register failed`:** search the PX4 log for
  `nros_rmw_uorb_register`; a non-zero return names what the build left out.
